title: Python for Data Science
description: Career roadmap from Python basics to pandas, statistics, SQL and machine learning for data analyst / data scientist roles.

skills.name: Python basics: syntax and types
keyPoints: Python is dynamically typed; common types: int, float, str, bool.
In Python 3, / always gives a float; // is floor division; % is remainder.
Strings are immutable; f-strings format values: f"{x:.2f}".
resources: NPTEL: The Joy of Computing using Python

items.stem: What is printed by print(type(3/2)) in Python 3?
items.explanation: True division always returns a float.

items.stem: What does 7 // 2 evaluate to in Python 3?
items.explanation: // is floor division.

skills.name: Conditionals and loops
keyPoints: range(start, stop, step) stops before 'stop'.
break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration; pass does nothing.
Prefer for-loops over sequences; use while when the number of iterations is unknown.

items.stem: How many values does `for i in range(2, 10, 3): print(i)` print?
items.explanation: It prints 2, 5, 8.

items.stem: Which keyword skips to the next iteration of a loop?
items.explanation: continue jumps to the next iteration.

skills.name: Functions and scope
keyPoints: A function without a return statement returns None.
Default argument values are evaluated once at definition time - avoid mutable defaults like [].
Variables assigned inside a function are local unless declared global/nonlocal.

items.stem:
def f(x, l=[]):
    l.append(x)
    return l
f(1)
print(f(2))  # prints?
items.explanation: The default list is created once and shared between calls.

items.stem: What does a Python function return if it has no return statement?
items.explanation: It implicitly returns None.

skills.name: Lists, dicts, sets and comprehensions
keyPoints: Lists are ordered and mutable; tuples are immutable.
Dictionary keys must be hashable (str, int, tuple of hashables) - lists and dicts cannot be keys.
Comprehension: [expr for x in seq if cond].

items.stem: What is [x*x for x in range(4) if x % 2 == 0]?
items.explanation: Even x in 0..3 are 0 and 2; squares 0 and 4.

items.stem: Which of these can be used as a dictionary key?
items.explanation: Only hashable (immutable) objects can be keys.

skills.name: Classes and objects
keyPoints: A class bundles data (attributes) and behaviour (methods).
__init__ initialises a new object's attributes; self refers to the current instance.
Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and override parent methods.

items.stem: In a Python method, self refers to:
items.explanation: self is the instance the method was called on.

items.stem: Which method initialises a new object's attributes?
items.explanation: __init__ runs after the object is created to set its attributes.

skills.name: NumPy arrays and vectorisation
keyPoints: NumPy arrays support element-wise arithmetic: np.array([1,2,3]) * 2 → [2,4,6].
Broadcasting stretches size-1 dimensions: (3,1) + (1,4) → (3,4).
Vectorised operations are much faster than Python loops.
resources: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (official docs)

items.stem: a = np.array([1, 2, 3]). What is a * 2?
items.explanation: Arithmetic on arrays is element-wise.

items.stem: What is the shape of np.zeros((3, 1)) + np.zeros((1, 4))?
items.explanation: Broadcasting expands both to (3, 4).

skills.name: pandas DataFrames
keyPoints: A DataFrame is a table of labelled columns (Series).
Boolean filtering: df[df['age'] > 30].
groupby + aggregation: df.groupby('city')['sales'].mean() gives one value per city.
.loc selects by label, .iloc by position.

items.stem: Which expression selects rows of df where column 'age' > 30?
items.explanation: A boolean Series inside [] filters rows; df.age > 30 alone is just the mask.

items.stem: df.groupby('city')['sales'].mean() returns:
options: Mean sales per city, as a Series
items.explanation: One aggregated value per group.

skills.name: Data visualisation
keyPoints: Histogram: distribution of one numeric variable.
Bar chart: compare a value across categories; line chart: trends over time; scatter: relationship of two numerics.
Label axes and units; avoid 3D and pie charts for comparisons.

items.stem: The best plot to show the distribution of a single numeric variable:
items.explanation: Histograms show distribution shape.

items.stem: To compare one numeric value across 5 categories, the clearest default is a:
items.explanation: Bars on a common baseline are easiest to compare.

skills.name: Descriptive statistics and probability
keyPoints: The median is robust to outliers; the mean is not.
Variance/standard deviation measure spread.
P(at least one) = 1 − P(none); independent events multiply.

items.stem: For data 2, 3, 3, 4, 100 the best measure of central tendency is the:
items.explanation: 100 is an outlier; the median (3) is robust.

skills.name: SQL for analysis
keyPoints: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE filters rows before grouping.
GROUP BY aggregates; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
COUNT(*) counts rows; JOINs combine tables on keys.

items.stem: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
items.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups.

items.stem: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t returns:
options: Non-null values in the first column
items.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows.

skills.name: Machine learning fundamentals
keyPoints: Supervised learning: regression predicts numbers, classification predicts categories.
Split data into train and test sets; fit on train, evaluate on test.
Overfitting: low training error, high test error; fix with more data, regularisation or simpler models.

items.stem: Predicting house price from features is an example of:
items.explanation: The target is a continuous number.

items.stem: A model has very low training error but high test error. This is:
items.explanation: It memorised training data and fails to generalise.

skills.name: Model evaluation and validation
keyPoints: Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data; use precision, recall, F1 or ROC-AUC.
k-fold cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate of generalisation.
Never tune hyper-parameters on the test set.

items.stem: For a rare-disease detector (1% positives), which metric is most misleading?
items.explanation: Predicting 'no disease' always gives 99% accuracy.

items.stem: Why use k-fold cross-validation?
options: To get a more reliable estimate of generalisation
items.explanation: Averaging over folds reduces variance of the estimate.
